title: Decouple priming and streaming handshake with warm-slice emulation
author: Elena Park
release_notes: Introduce a warm-slice emulation mode and decouple KV priming from streaming decode handshake to reduce tail latency for short interactive requests and improve kernel scheduling efficiency.
description:
Summary: This PR separates model "priming" (what we previously called prefill) from continuous streaming/decoding handshake, introducing a warm-slice emulation mode and a light-weight priming scheduler. The goal is to reduce tail latency and jitter for short interactive workloads while keeping high throughput for long-running streams.

Motivation: We observed that tightly coupling priming and decode streaming causes contention in the kernel scheduler and excessive KV cache churn for short queries that rarely exhaust a full decode window. Two common bad outcomes were: (1) short requests incur extra decode scheduling latency waiting for large priming windows to finish, and (2) speculative priming triggered large KV writes that pushed useful tokens out of fast-tier cache.

Approach:
- Introduce an explicit "priming" stage distinct from the streaming/decode stage. Priming performs model context construction and KV warmup without holding decode kernel resources.
- Add warm-slice emulation: a lightweight priming path that builds KV fragments sized to an emulated decode slice (configurable, default 64 tokens) and writes them with soft-admission into the KV cache. Warm-slice emulation avoids full kernel prefill runs for short requests.
- Implement a PrimingScheduler that tracks token-lane priorities (interactive vs batch), estimated decode windows, and memory pressure signals from KV cache. The scheduler admits priming fragments opportunistically and can abort/resume priming when decode demand spikes.
- Flow control changes: the streaming handshake now checks for a primed slice fingerprint instead of assuming prefill completion. If the primed fingerprint exists, decode proceeds immediately; otherwise decode triggers a short inline priming fallback.
- Metrics and tracing: new metrics priming.latency_ms, priming.kv_writes, priming.aborts and traces that link priming fragments to subsequent decode kernels for end-to-end visibility.

Commits (high-level):
- 1a2b3c4: add priming scheduler and warm-slice emulation shims
- 2b3c4d5: move KV write logic into priming worker; add soft-admit API
- 3c4d5e6: streaming handshake rework to consult priming fingerprint
- 4d5e6f7: metrics/tracing + unit tests
- 5e6f7g8: e2e bench harness and microbench results + docs

Changes made (selected files):
- runtime/scheduler/priming_scheduler.rs: new scheduler implementation and admission heuristics
- runtime/kv/kv_writer.rs: soft-admit writes, fragment metadata, eviction hints
- runtime/stream/handshake.rs: consult priming fingerprint and inline fallback path
- runtime/metrics/priming_metrics.rs: new metrics and tag propagation
- tests/bench/priming_vs_stream_latency.py: end-to-end synthetic benchmarks
- docs/ops/priming.md: operational guidance for the mode and rollout strategy

Small illustrative snippet (priming API):

// priming worker: emit a KV fragment with soft admission
priming_worker.emit_fragment(fragment_id, payload, SoftAdmission::Try);

Benchmarks:
- Short interactive synthetic workload (median request 8 tokens, 95th percentile response tokens 32): tail latency improvement: 95th ms reduced by 28% (from 124ms -> 89ms), p99 reduced by 20%.
- Mixed workload with bursty decodes: overall throughput unchanged within noise (+0.6%), KV write rate down by ~12% under interactive-heavy traffic due to soft admission.
- Long streaming workloads (typical >512 tokens): no regression observed; small improvement in kernel scheduling fairness in specific cases where priming previously blockaded decode threads.

Testing and CI:
- Unit tests added for scheduler heuristics and priming fingerprint correctness.
- Integration tests exercise inline fallback and soft admission under simulated KV pressure.
- Bench harness added to tests/bench to reproduce numbers above.

CI run: full pipeline passed; a flaky e2e was retried once and succeeded.

Review thread (condensed):
- Samir: requested stronger invariants around fragment fingerprint collisions; added a unique nonce per priming epoch and improved tests.
- Aisha: asked for clearer metrics (split priming.kv_writes into admitted vs rejected); changed accordingly.
- Markus: found an edge-case where inline fallback could double-prime if a race occurs; author added a small CAS and re-ran benchmarks.
- Author replies: fixed collision and race issues, documented failure modes in docs/ops/priming.md.

Operational notes and rollout:
- Feature gated behind "warm_slice_emulation" config flag (default off in main).
- Canary rollout plan: enable for 5% of interactive traffic in staging, monitor priming.kv_writes.admitted, priming.aborts, latency.p95 and decode.queue_length.
- If admitted KV writes rise above preset thresholds under constrained caches, revert to conservative admission.

Backwards compatibility and safety:
- No protocol change to client APIs. The handshake semantics are strictly additive: if priming fingerprint is absent, the system falls back to the existing inline priming path.
- Soft-admit ensures that KV writes do not evict critical cache entries aggressively.
- A telemetry-based automatic rollback is in place for the first 72 hours of canary.

Known limitations and future work:
- Current warm-slice default size (64 tokens) is conservative; we plan an adaptive slice size experiment driven by request length distributions.
- The warm-slice path reduces but does not eliminate KV churn for pathological workloads with many mid-length requests; we will evaluate combining this with a microbatch coalescer.
- More aggressive kernel-level hints (per-fragment kernel affinity) are left to a follow-up to keep this PR bounded.

Related work: This complements earlier work on decode handoff and microchunking by separating responsibilities and adding a low-cost priming path for short-lived requests (see ENG-3421 and ENG-4153 for tracking tasks).
